Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I be happy alone?
Answer: When I was younger, I was under the impression that I needed other people to be happy. A few years after that, I began to believe that the only person that could make me happy was myself. Now, I’ve realized that the issue isn’t so black or white. Happiness is a bit complicated. You need other people, and you also need to take care of yourself. Here’s a random picture of when my sister and I had breakfast the other day. We’re weird. People love to romanticize their independence. I know because I’ve done it, I’ve seen people around me do it, and I’m a part of a culture where being “self-sufficient” is seen as the crown jewel of personal development. If you can take care of yourself, you’re supposed to be “safe”. No one can hurt you if you “love yourself”. You’re supposed to be completely self-sufficient — financially, spiritually, emotionally, and physically. When you can take care of yourself, they say that you’re supposed to be “good”. But you’re not. For the last year, I’ve been on a personal mission to create a life where I’m able to take care of myself, feel free from dependence on others, and make a living doing what I love (while traveling, going on adventures, and doing other fun stuff). I created this life, and I’m realizing now that this was only the first step in what I’ve really wanted out of my life. I don’t want to be “happy” the way it looks in the movies. A few weeks ago, I went on a really nice vacation in Italy. I spent 2 nights in Rome, 2 in a small town off the Amalfi Coast called Vietri Sul Mare, and another one in Naples. I ate pizza, drank wine, walked around, looked at a bunch of old buildings, went to the beach, and had a really nice time. But it was insanely difficult, especially the first couple of days. I missed teaching Jiu-Jitsu. I missed training. I missed trying to improve my skills in writing and Jiu-Jitsu every day. Sure, it was nice to take a break and I made an effort to enjoy every moment of it, but I had to force myself to take a break. I had to force myself to not hustle. It was really nice to not cut weight and eat pizza every day instead of salads and chicken and broccoli, but drowning yourself in wine and carbs is not real life. Fulfillment doesn’t come from bread, fulfillment comes from doing the hard stuff to make the break. A meaningful life comes from challenges. So why shouldn’t you just work yourself into the ground? It’s actually selfish to burn yourself out. In the early parts of my career as an athlete, I felt disgustingly selfish in my own skin. I’ve always had to prioritize training and work over friendships, relationships, and even my own financial security. I’ve had to make a lot of sacrifices to be decent at what I do, and the result has been a growing amount of self-sufficiency and a great deal of anxiety. After working my butt off at martial arts for more than a decade, I’m finally good enough to make a living teaching, fighting, and now, writing about it. So why am I not happy? I think it’s because the “grind” does not make me happy. I don’t “embrace the grind” because these periods of intense internal hustle, constant pushing, and the discovery of my own limits are not what make my life meaningful. What really makes me happy is giving back. Taking care of myself is cool and essential and I’m glad that I can do that, but there’s another step. I need to give back. I need to help people. Working on myself has been lovely. I feel proud of everything I’ve accomplished, and I’m going to keep working to accomplish more, but fulfillment doesn’t come from working hard at stuff alone. Fulfillment comes from working hard at stuff and then helping other people to do the same. To me, fulfillment means making the path easier for others to follow. Give them tools you never had. Taking care of yourself is cool, but you can do better than that. Self-improvement is not inherently selfish, but a lot of people make it that way. Working on yourself and meditating and journaling and doing all that stuff is a solo activity designed to enhance your individual experience, but there’s more to life than just making your own life better. Yes, you’re born alone. Yes, you die alone. However, just about every moment that you spend engaged in this world is deeply connected with other beings. Just like on an airplane, after you can take care of yourself, it’s time to work on helping take care of other people. However, what seems like happens often is that people become obsessed with their own improvement. They become obsessed with reading self-help, they become obsessed with improving themselves, and they never take the time to actually help make the world a better place. It’s as if they have a beautiful garden in a crappy town. Here’s the truth: if the world around you is on fire, it doesn’t matter if you’re driving a Bentley or a Toyota, you’re still going to burn. Some people devote their lives to service from a young age. I don’t think that’s right either, because if you make an effort to help the world but can’t actually help yourself, you become a net negative to the world because people have to spend their own resources trying to clean up your mess. To put it in martial arts terms, if I opened up my own dojo with only 6 months of training and tried to scam people (intentionally or not, it doesn’t matter) into buying lessons from me despite my incompetence, these people would eventually have to spend more money to buy more lessons from better people to correct their bad habits. Their future instructors would have to invest more time into trying to fix them. Even if I had the best intentions, I’d be a net negative in the world because of my incompetence. That’s why you have to have both for a complete existence. You have to take care of yourself, and you have to give back to the community. At this point in time, I can’t think of a better way to live.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Where do I start to get my life together?
Answer: When I was 17, I was severely depressed, chronically anxious, and lost as to what I was going to do with my life. Then, a few weeks before I graduated high school, I started learning Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. What happened next is a long journey and an even longer story that spans 8 years, from the time I was an anxious schooler to today, where I’m 25, doing what I love full-time, having great mental health, and “living the dream”. Living my dream. It’s partially because of Jiu-Jitsu, partially because of writing, and partially because of my disciplined effort over years and years. Here’s what happened: This story has been told before, and it will be told again. You’ve probably read or heard a story like this one before — about someone who was a mess and how martial arts (or some other craft) “saved their life”. But I wasn’t a mess. I was a decent high school wrestler, I was going to college, and I was dating my high school sweetheart. I was doing okay, but I was just lost, sad, and more anxious than I could possibly understand. I wasn’t a mess, I was just having a hard time. I was having a hard time until I started to learn Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Jiu-Jitsu became the band-aid for all of my personal problems and anxieties, and I drank the Kool-Aid (and a lot of it). After I started competing in Jiu-Jitsu, my grappling addiction took over my life. I moved back in with my parents, started training full-time, and “punted” everything else. I started winning tournaments and matches at the lower belts of Jiu-Jitsu. I became pretty good. However, my early success didn’t last. I started to struggle. My mental health was catching up with me. My neck, my back, my anxiety attacks. Around that time, the depression that I’d been treating with a big ole Jiu-Jitsu band-aid started to seep through into my personal life. I had toxic relationship after toxic relationship. I cheated on my partners. I dropped out of college and then re-enrolled — twice. I failed my exercise science program and had to choose a new major. I couldn’t keep a part-time job without butting heads with my bosses. I wasn’t really doing anything well in my life, but I had a decent armbar. Then, in the midst of a series of serious physical injuries, a few tough defeats on the mat, and some other personal issues at home, I spiraled out of control. I experienced a rare mental condition called “depersonalization”, and at 21, I came close to committing suicide. I even wrote a note. Then, 12 months after I wrote a suicide note in my parent’s basement, I won the IBJJF No-Gi Worlds at purple belt. This was a great moment, but it made me realize how naive I was being about so much in my life. Winning the tournament was both inspiring and humbling. It was inspiring because it taught me that I was capable of a lot more than I thought. It was humbling because I realized that for the most part, no one gave a shit. I realized that I was fighting for myself (and only myself) and that selfishness wasn’t a sustainable source of motivation. On paper, the biggest win of my life didn’t change my life at all. That’s when I started to grow. After winning the Worlds, I was also now 22, and my friends were getting jobs, living in nicer apartments, and some were even getting married. I was a Jiu-Jitsu bum who couldn’t see anything past his next tournament. In my old circle of friends, Jiu-Jitsu went from being my cool hobby to a reason that I wasn’t growing up. I drank the Jiu-Jitsu Kool-Aid so hard that now, I was choking on it. After this, I became incredibly interested in ways to make a living while doing Jiu-Jitsu, instead of making a living from doing Jiu-Jitsu. I started to leverage the only other skill I sort of had: writing. After a few months of helplessly trying to freelance, I started a blog on Medium at the end of 2020. Within a few months, I became obsessed with writing. I wrote about everything I could think about — from Jiu-Jitsu to philosophy to love to mindset. I wrote about stuff I knew and stuff I didn’t. I wrote a lot. And? In time, with practice, patience, and a lot of hard work, I became a writer. Writing gave me a new identity and a new job, and it also taught me what Jiu-Jitsu is really about. I fell in love with writing as deeply as I fell with Jiu-Jitsu, and I found myself in a strange position. I was the only person competing at the higher levels of Jiu-Jitsu who was also writing about it (and making money from it). For a while, I felt like I was cheating reality. After a while, I realized that I was happy with what I was doing. I was so fucking happy. The more I wrote, the harder I trained, and the better I got at both of my passions. Eventually, I gained more than 10 million views on my online writing and became ranked in the top 15 in the world in Jiu-Jitsu. Now, I write/ghostwrite professionally, teach Jiu-Jitsu, and compete in professional Jiu-Jitsu events. Though I’m not exactly where I want to be, in a way, I made it. I forget that sometimes. That’s pretty cool to me. But what’s the point? I’m happy. So what? This article isn’t really about me. I’m the writer so I get to be the main character of my own story, but this story is not about me. This story is about life, love, and learning. That’s what writing is about. That’s what Jiu-Jitsu is supposed to be about. I see a lot of bullshit online about how “writing saved my life” or “Jiu-Jitsu saved my life”. Give yourself some credit — a craft doesn’t make or break your existence. Jiu-Jitsu didn’t “save my life”, but it did give me a framework to grow up into a person I’m proud to be. It also gave me a job, a sense of purpose, and a great set of friends. Writing gave me all that, and the ability to tell stories about the stuff I do. That’s how I got my shit together. Hopefully, this isn’t just me ranting and praising my own hard work. Hopefully, this helped you a bit. Have a great day.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What overly simplistic life advice is deceptively effective if used correctly?
Answer: “Don’t give up.” I used to hate being told to not give up. I thought that being told to keep going was annoying, obvious, and even kind of toxic. Hustle Porn tells you to not give up. Stupid posters with mountains and clouds tell you to not give up. That random dude on Quora who has tape around his head tells you not to give up in like half his answers… 😁 However, in terms of improvement and development, the single act of “not giving up” will transform your odds of success. Someone who’s impossible to kill is tough to beat. For my entire life, all I’ve really wanted to do was just give up on things. For a while, I didn’t just want to give up on things. I wanted to give up on life. I was suicidal. I hate saying that because it’s almost cliche and uninteresting that a self-help-ish writer would have a period with suicidal depression, so I’m sorry in advance for being lame and typical. I just want to be honest with you. One thing I’ve never regretted is not giving up. I’ve competed in martial arts tournaments with torn knees, torn shoulders, herniated discs, mental illness, and hardly any money in my bank account (you know, which I’d need to pay rent and other “life stuff” apart from chasing my real-life Dragon Ball quest), and 9 times out of 10, this resilience has made me happier, more confident, and yes, more successful. Days before I won my world championship in Jiu-Jitsu, I was asking my friends if it was okay if I could quit Jiu-Jitsu. I almost didn’t compete in this tournament a few weeks ago because my back was fucked, but I did anyway and I won $5000 and beat one of the top athletes in the world in my sport. Before some of the biggest moments in my life, I’ve been pacing through my mind begging for a way to escape. Begging for a way out. I’ve also given up a bunch of times, too. While some of the “quits” that I’ve made have been great for me (I’ve quit some toxic relationships and quit some careers that were going nowhere), not quitting has been far more important for developing my character and improving myself. If you quit, that’s it. But what happens if you don’t? In many cases, it’s well worth spinning the wheel and trying to find out. Here’s my newsletter. If you like my writing and want to read more, check it out. We’d love to have you. 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Share something you're grateful for today?
Answer: Here’s a picture of my dad and me from the 2016 IBJJF No-Gi World Jiu-Jitsu Championships. This was the first-ever world championship tournament that I competed in. I was a 19-year-old blue belt. When I signed up for this tournament, if I’m being completely honest, I didn’t know the rules of Jiu-Jitsu. I was really scared. By some luck of the draw (literally, I got a lucky draw in the bracket that made winning matches a bit easier), I managed to take 3rd place in the world championship with about a year of Jiu-Jitsu training under my belt. I was living in Oregon at the time, and my dad flew all the way out from Chicago just to watch me compete. He didn’t coach me. He didn’t yell at me. He didn’t give me a motivational speech. He just hung out with me for the weekend. My dad is not a “wrestling-dad”. My mom was not a “wrestling-mom”. My parents were never emotionally invested in my athletic career, but they also supported it. I’m incredibly grateful for that. Here’s why: Last night, I was teaching my kids Jiu-Jitsu class, and one of the guys who I was coaching with started screaming at his son during the class. He embarrassed his son in front of all his friends, all of the other students, and all of the parents watching the class. The worst part is, he didn't think of it this way. He thought he was “toughening him up”. I hadn’t noticed it before, but it occurred to me last night that he does that pretty often, and it also occurred to me that the kid probably doesn't love being yelled at by my dad every time he makes a wrong move at Jiu-Jitsu practice. When I wrestled as a kid, my parents never told me what to do on the mat. They never wrestled, and any advice that had was going to be counterintuitive. They were smart enough to know that. My parents made me tough in other ways. My childhood was easy in a lot of ways, but I still had some challenges. I went to a good school. I grew up in a 2 parent household. I got to play sports throughout high school. But still, emotionally, a lot of things were hard. My dad has a lot of trauma from his youth, and he struggles with it a lot. He didn’t exactly learn how to talk about or deal with mental health from his abusive parents who both had severe drinking problems. This makes it hard for him to control his emotions. It makes him drink more than he should to cope with his PTSD. My dad isn’t perfect, but compared to the situation he was raised in, he’s a hero. He also taught me some really important lessons. My dad showed me how to be tough by going through life and thriving despite all of the pain that he has experienced. He also showed me that you can go through hell and come out the other side a kind person. He showed me that you can be tough and thoughtful. Kind and strong. Here’s me and my mom from a trip we took to New York for a Jiu-Jitsu tournament in 2017. I won 2 gold medals and a $400 cash prize this weekend. It was one of the first times I won money in sports. I felt really proud because I paid for her flight and for our Airbnb on this trip. My mom is tough as fuck. She swam a mile the day before I was born. My mom taught me how to be tough by beating breast cancer when I was just 4 years old. She taught me to be tough by being tough herself. One of my earliest memories (I was about 4 or 5) is going into the bathroom of our house to pee one night and finding my mom and dad, both covered in blood, tending to the wounds from one of the surgeries she had. It was a bit shocking, and that was a really hard period for my family, but we got through it. My parents taught me how to get through shit. Sometimes, when you are getting through shit, it hurts. Sometimes you yell. Sometimes you scream. Sometimes you cuss. Sometimes you cry into a pillow. You’re allowed to do all those things. You just don’t quit, unless you’ve got a damn good reason to. I don't want to sound like I’m romanticizing anything, but my parents are tough as fuck, and I’m glad that they didn’t ruin my favorite sport while trying to instill mental strength into my brain. I’m grateful for my mom and dad because they taught me a lot of incredible lessons over the years. They taught me how to be tough. They taught me to be a good person. They also backed off and let me make my own failures. My hobbies were my hobbies. My sport was my sport. My career is my career. My anxiety is my anxiety. I have to deal with my shit if I want to be okay. No one is coming to save me. In a generation of helicopter parents, I appreciate the fact that I was allowed to fall flat on my face a bunch because I’ve learned a lot from those experiences. My parents taught me that you can be successful and imperfect. You can be fucked up and that makes you perfect. My mom and dad and I aren’t as close as we used to be, but maybe that’s just part of trying to be your own person. I guess this is growing up. I’m also grateful for my sister (my sea star) because one day, she’s all that I’ll have left.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What do fit people think about overweight people at the gym?
Answer: When I think about overweight people at the gym, I feel happy for them. I want them to keep going to the gym. To keep doing things that are good for their physical health. The worst part of the fitness industry is its unnecessary exclusivity. The amount of body-shaming that happens in fitness is insane. But at the same time, for better or for worse, I don’t think much about overweight people at the gym. I feel like it’d be weird if I had a really strong opinion on this either way. Overweight people are just other people who are also at the gym. I don’t think about the other people at the gym unless they’re taking an obnoxious amount of selfies or screaming/grunting. When I’m at the gym, I mostly try to focus on myself, think about ideas that have been circulating through my mind, do my workout, and then go home. That’s just me.
